utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are following our hearings. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. You have the floor, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I note you have binder 2, which I recall the Judges would like binder 2, as we have them here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, we are looking forward to receiving them. We are dreaming on them already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're collecting ourselves I'll -- we left off yesterday in the narrative of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I take it that the Defence is in the possession of the binder as well. Is that correct, Mr. Gajic? I see you nodding. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. We had left off in the documentary narrative where the Srebrenica enclave had been created by the Security Council. There was a VRS attack planned for Zepa and Gorazde which, according to Mr. Butler, didn't really go very far because the Zepa enclaves were -- the Zepa enclave and Gorazde was created. So now I would take us into the year, and we won't spend much time in this year, in 1994. If we could go to P2158. It should be 44 of the tab. And this is a document the Trial Chamber has seen at least one or two times, I think, so I won't spend a lot of time on it, but it is a document from the Bratunac Brigade Command, dated 4 July 1994, entitled "Report for the Brigade Members." So we can see what that is. And if we can go to page 2 in the English and it should be page 3 in the B/C/S. Actually, it was the previous page in the B/C/S. If we go back one in the B/C/S, we should catch it. Yeah, that's where it is. And we're going to need to go to the next -- well, soon the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's this section that the Court has heard before that I want to ask you about: "We have won the war in Podrinje," and I think you've explained where that is already, "but we have not beaten the Muslims completely, which is what we must do in the next period. We must obtain our final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje. The enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde must be defeated militarily." Now, Mr. Butler, briefly, to your knowledge, were there military -- Muslim military activities coming out of those enclaves during this time that the Serb forces felt like they needed to engage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on to say: "We must continue to arm, train, discipline and prepare the RS Army for the execution of this crucial task, the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." I think that speaks for itself. Then it says: "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." In your view, does this include or not include a reference to civilians?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're not specifically noting just the military forces, so as a result I read this as they are also including the surrounding civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's -- if we just look at the end of this document, we see that it's from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade at the time, Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic. As a brigade commander -- in your opinion, would a brigade commander be able to give this direction to his troops on his own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. He's receiving guidance from higher levels of command. And, again, when one looks at this particular document, it is drafted specifically to provide information not only to lower levels of the brigade, but actually to individual members of the brigade, as the leadership of the army explains out in detail, the objectives of the war in a way and in a manner that each soldier can understand. So this isn't something that the brigade is doing in isolation. This is something -- part of a larger strategy in order to positively influence the morale of the soldiers, not only the Bratunac Brigade but of all the military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 1 of this document. And we can see that it begins by saying: "During his recent visit to the corps command, the commander of the VRS indicated that he would soon visit some of the corps units, including the Bratunac Brigade." Now, you say this brigade commander would not have received this -- would not have done this on his own. Where, along the chain of command, should he have received -- who should he have received this direction from before he passed it on to his troops?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all probability, he would have received guidance relating to this from the Drina Corps Command; more specifically, the Drina Corps assistant commander for Morale and Religious Affairs at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would the Drina Corps, in your view, have been able to enunciate a policy to expel the Muslims of Srebrenica on their own or would they have -- would they have received direction from someone else or some other body?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. My view is that they would have received their guidance in this regard from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Lieutenant-Colonel Ognjenovic, can you tell us where he went after his stint as the Bratunac Brigade commander or where he was in July 1995, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After completing his tour as the commander -- or his stint as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and I believe it was May 1995, he then went back to the Drina Corps, and he was an operations officer or a member of their operations staff in July of 1995 at the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue on to the next document, which I believe is 65 ter 31. And we're now -- or at last getting into 1995 in our narrative. And we can see that we have a document from the Main Staff, Intelligence and Security Sector, dated 19 March 1995. We can see from the original that it's in the name of General Tolimir, and we see from the initials "ZT" of the drafter, which, as I think you've told us, that should be drafted by General Tolimir. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see in this document, it's entitled "The Establishment of the Security System and Control of the Territory," and the first paragraph talks about the area of Konjevic Polje and the forces based there to establish a security system. It talks about Cerska, Udric, Glogova, places we're all familiar with. Then the next paragraph says: "Because of the need to engage the VRS units at the front of the SRK and the Drina Corps, we are forced to relocate the unit based in Konjevic Polje ..." Can you tell us what General Tolimir is doing in this document, what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular point in time, particularly the Drina Corps is completely stretched with regards to available manpower and units, and particularly those units that are surrounding the enclaves, maintaining the outer perimeter, if you will. In March of 1995, a particular situation arose on the Sarajevo battle-front where they had to re-allocate units to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, in effect creating a gap between military positions held between the Bratunac Brigade and the Milici Brigade, a gap which the Bosnian Muslim military forces can and did exploit. So in this context, the army, the Main Staff, is requesting that the Ministry of the Interior be tasked to provide police forces to cover that specific segment of the gap, in light of the security threat that, you know, the opening of that gap has created to the surrounding population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you seen documents that indicate that the Bosnian Muslim army had a particular policy and strategy to engage the military outside of Srebrenica in order to tie down Serb forces, to prevent them from going to the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. The -- one of the stated missions of the 28th Infantry Division was to conduct military operations in such a manner that it would force the VRS to maintain military forces surrounding the enclaves rather than have the ability to redeploy those forces to what it considered to be more critical areas of the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the -- was this action by the 28th Division, inside the enclave, going outside the enclave, in your view, a violation of the demilitarised agreement that was in place at -- when the enclaves were formed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly, it was, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at this document, we see that the general is referring to -- and I would say the second page in English is what I'm looking at especially. He's making very specific references to Birac, Podrinje, Milici, Konjevic Polje. What would this indicate to you about General Tolimir's knowledge of the geography and the strategic importance of this area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects that he is quite well versed in the military geography, where the Drina Corps units are, where there are potential gaps in the line, and what the military threat those particular gaps represent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 31 shall be assigned Exhibit P2498. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. On the same subject, could we go to 65 ter 00007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for that to come up: We will soon see that this is from the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior, the Cabinet of the Minister, and it's to the president of the Republika Srpska, Dr. Karadzic, and someone has signed for the minister, Zivko Rakic. What is this, and how does it fit in with -- if at all, with what we just saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is the response of the Ministry of the Interior back to the president, and further through the army, informing them that based on their request, the police have dispatched the 2nd PJP or Police Company from the Zvornik Public Security Centre to that area, where they will be responsible for establishing control over the security of the various roads that are listed there. So this is, in effect, the Ministry of the Interior stepping up to provide forces to deal with the previously-mentioned threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see a reference to: "We have dispatched the 2nd Company of the PJP of the Zvornik Public Security Centre." Now, are we going to be hearing more information about the 2nd Company of the PJP as we get to the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, particularly in the period following the attack on Srebrenica. Because of their physical location on the battle-field, that particular unit has a number of interactions with individuals who are captured later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how a PJP unit is assembled? What is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the normal police functions that were undertaken by the Ministry of the Interior, they were also expected, as a component part of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, to be able to engage in combat activities, to a limited extent, when necessary. In order to accomplish this, what each CSB or Sector for Security did was to take its existing municipal police forces and organise them in a series of mobilisation companies that could be called up at a time when they were needed to perform combat or combat-related operations. These were not permanent establishments. They were designed to be called up as needed. The way that it was organised in the Zvornik Security Sector was a total of six companies, the first company being organised out of the youngest and fittest of the police officers, and by the time you got to the fourth, fifth and final company, you're getting to the oldest and least capable of the police officers. So by organising in this manner, you could quickly put together the requisite company-sized military force that you needed, but you could also do so in a way that you did not completely take all of the police out of a certain region. Some of the members of the company would come from Bratunac, some from Milici, some from Vlasenica, Zvornik, so that when you mobilise one of these companies for combat activities, you didn't denude a certain area completely of police coverage. So this was how the police in the sectors -- in the security sectors -- or the public safety sectors organised themselves to be able to also perform military-related duties on an ad hoc basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one follow-up question to that. Sir, you just explained how these PJP units were composed and established. Was that, in the Republika Srpska, done in the same way as in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, sir. I'm not aware of and I just haven't looked at the issue of how, in the former Yugoslavia, the police were organised or put into the military, so I just don't have the ability to answer that question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see, in this document, that the translation -- the translation side in the English has noted that "PJP" meant "Special Police Unit," and the Court has heard quite a bit of evidence about Ljubisa Borovcanin as the deputy commander of the RS Special Police and their activities around Kravica, the location there, and in Srebrenica, as he was the subject of the Petrovic video in some degree. Can you tell us, this English translation as "Special Police Unit," has this anything to do with the Republika Srpska Special Police units that were commanded at the time in Srebrenica by Ljubisa Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular Special Police Unit is part of the Special Police Brigade that answered directly to the Ministry of the Interior. So in that sense, the best way, perhaps, to describe it is that the PJP units answered directly to the head of the Sector for Security, in this case the Zvornik CSB, while the Special Police units, if you've heard the 2nd Sekovici Detachment Special Police Unit, those answered directly to the Special Police Brigade and then the Ministry of the Interior. So while they're both Special Police units, they are subordinated to different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for your knowledge, the term "PJP" and the term "Special Police" are two different words in the Serbian language, but English ended up translating them as both "Special." So this lends to -- has lent to quite a bit of confusion over the years, so we tried just to use the abbreviation "PJP" so we don't get them mixed up with the Special Police, as Mr. Butler has described. I'm sure Mr. Gajic will agree with me on that point. And we will get more into the detail as we see some more documents on that. So I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7 shall be assigned Exhibit P2499. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Butler, if we could go to P1214, known as Directive 7. Could we go -- we see in the English that, if you recall, this is where the translations got slightly mixed up. Could we go to the next page in the English, because that's the -- as you may recall, that's the cover page by which this document was sent out. All right. And the document was sent out -- the cover page, as you just saw, was dated 17 March 1995, but this first page, we can see, Mr. Butler, that this is dated 8 March 1995, and it's -- we see the title "Directive for Further Operations, OP Number 7." Is this related to the kind of directive that you talked about before when you talked about Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's exactly a continuation of the series of directives that were published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this document, I think we can all agree, at the last page of the document we see that it's in the -- it was drafted by Colonel Miletic, but it's in the name of the supreme commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Can you explain why, I believe, Directive 4 was in the name of the -- General Mladic, this is in the name of President Karadzic, and what do you make of that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very early year of the war -- years of the war, the political bodies, to a large degree, allowed the military to draft the strategic plans based on very general political guidance. As the war progressed and as the Supreme Command, as it were, became more experienced and took a greater hand in directing the war effort, they took a larger role in overseeing the strategic -- the creation of the strategic plans to ensure that they were aligned with the political objectives of the state. So in this particular situation, which made it different from Directive 4, which was strictly the military drafted it and published it, in this particular case you have Directive 7, which although drafted by the military, is approved by the political leadership of the state. And then what you'll see is a more detailed version of Directive 7, known as Directive 7/1, which the military itself then drafts to provide amplifying guidance to military units and corps commanders. So, I mean, this is just a mature -- a maturing of the military/political apparatus of the Republika Srpska as time goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page -- as we know, these are divided up by different tasks to the different corps. Is that correct? Like Directive 4, Directive 7 is setting out tasks for the various corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 10 in the English and page 15 of the B/C/S, which is the Drina Corps section, which the Court has seen many times. And just to call your attention to the section, in the middle of the page: "While in the direction of Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, complete physical separation of Srebrenica from Zepa should be carried out as soon as possible, preventing even communication between individuals in the two enclaves." Can you tell us what that means and why, if you know, the VRS would have made this an objective, that one sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Because of the terrain and a lack of manpower, as discussed earlier, particularly the Drina Corps could not completely encircle both enclaves. As a result, it was well known that individual soldiers, civilians, military supplies, could travel over land through various valleys and paths from the Srebrenica enclave to the Zepa enclave and then back. So as any part of ultimately militarily defeating the Muslim forces in the enclave, they recognised that they were going to have to block those paths to be able to keep people from being able -- people and supplies from being able to physically move back and forth between the Zepa enclave and the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is your view on whether or not this objective was a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular aspect is certainly a legitimate objective, to cut the lines of communications between two military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me continue the next part: "By planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of the Srebrenica and Zepa." What, in your view, is this -- does this mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the phrase "inhabitants," in my view, encompasses both military and civilian population, this is where you start to cross the line and you start to make the civilian population in those areas part of the objects of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when it says "by planned and well-thought-out combat operations, create an unbearable situation," in your view, does that include -- is that suggesting a plan to take out the entire enclaves is an objective at this point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- at this point in time, I do not believe that their intention is to actually physically take over the enclaves at this juncture. What I believe that they are attempting to do at this point in time is to create the conditions similar to they had in April of -- May in 1993, whereby compressing the enclaves into smaller and smaller areas and creating that type of humanitarian crisis, it forces the United Nations, themselves, to declare that the enclaves are not tenable and to evacuate them themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this next sentence -- how do you read the next sentence in this -- in your evaluation? And we need to, I'm sorry, go over to the next page in English. Thank you. "In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps Command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively liberating the Drina Valley region." So how does that fit into your previous opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I incorporate that line, as well as other language in Directive 7, that I believe we're going to get into in a bit, as all part of my analysis that at this point in time, the objective wasn't to militarily conquer the enclaves, it was to create the conditions where the United Nations forces would come to the conclusion that they could not sustain the enclaves and that the impetus would then be on the United Nations to end the enclaves and remove the populations themselves. This, in fact, was just part of it, that the military was being instructed that should the United Nations abandon the enclaves, that they should be prepared to rapidly engage in military activities against any remaining BiH Army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You mention another part of the directive. Let's go to -- should be Serbian page 21, page 14 in the English. But before we get to this section, let me ask you: From that last section and the Drina Corps, in your military opinion, would General Tolimir, who was, as we know, the chief of Intel and Security at the time, would he have been aware of this directive and aware of the specific language that we've just gone over for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he would have had to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inherent in both Directive 7 and in the supplemental Directive 7/1, there are a number of specific tasks which the security branch will have to be a part of in order to realise these plans not only for the Drina Corps but for all of the corps, so he has to be aware of what the general political/military objectives are in great detail in order to ensure that he can synchronise the work of the Sector for Intelligence and Security to support those missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remind us, just briefly, what it is that he would be doing to support those missions, in particular? I mean -- well, not particular facts, but what would his job be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His portfolio, as the assistant commander for Intelligence and Security, would cover all of those aspects related to, for example, with the enclaves, monitoring the United Nations presence and their willingness to continue to remain in those enclaves is going to be a classic intelligence function. The intelligence organs of the various military units, and particularly the Main Staff, is going to be responsible for obtaining information relating to the United Nations' willingness to continue these missions. From the security perspective, one making sure that what the actual plan and intent of in the VRS remains camouflaged from the United Nations or the international community is going to require the work of his security sector and counter-intelligence to make sure that they don't leak information that would be of detriment to this plan. So he has to be aware of what the plan is in great detail in order to ensure that the Sector for Intelligence and Security can implement all of the missions that they are going to be required to do in order to support these objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that gets us to the next section which is under the larger heading of "Support for Combat Operations," and the smaller heading, "The Morale" -- or "Moral and Psychological Support." If we could go down to the fourth paragraph, and it says: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively-restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependent on our good will while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." Now, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence about convoys and supplies, and issues that were being faced in this regard. Can you tell us, Mr. Butler, who is being targeted by this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The declared target is the UNPROFOR and their ability to resupply the enclaves, but it makes it clear that ultimately the target or the people who are going to feel the impact is going to be the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think they meant by "reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As time goes on, and it actually started, literally, a month or two earlier, what begins to become clear is a pattern where the UNPROFOR forces in the enclaves are -- their combat and other abilities to protect the enclaves are degradated [sic] as a result of a policy of not letting the UN units resupply personnel, resupply equipment that has been damaged or is broken, and to resupply logistics, ammunition utilisation, particularly personnel rotation through the units when their tour of duty is completed. And by doing this over a sustained period of time, you greatly impact the combat ability of the United Nations units to perform their missions. That is what this particular paragraph discusses. And when one looks in the intervening months at what happened to the United Nations Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica, you'll be able to see the complete manifestation of that plan and how it impacted or limited the Dutch Battalion's ability to do their missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did fuel play a role in any of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did. In fact, fuel became so acute for the Dutch Battalion that they were forced to abandon patrols of various areas of the enclaves simply because they did not have enough fuel for their armoured vehicles to go on patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what purpose does disabling UNPROFOR in this way serve, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: By limiting UNPROFOR's mobility, one, militarily UNPROFOR can no longer effectively police the safe area and prevent either Bosnian Serb or Bosnian Muslim military operations from occurring, and the second is that by degrading the UN's operations and its ability to protect itself, it has a significantly adverse impact on the UN's ability to sustain the civilian population within the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, P1199, and we can see that this is now Directive 7.1. And is this what you had been referring to earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this document in any way negate or undermine Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. It -- in fact, it is -- it amplifies and supplements Directive 7 with more specific tasks for the units to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we'll all agree that in Directive 7/1 there's no discussion specifically related to the enclaves, or making life impossible for the Muslims, or reducing the logistics support and the humanitarian aid in this document. Does that suggest to you anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it doesn't suggest to me that they've abandoned the mission. It just simply is a reflection of the more specific military tasks that are outlined in 7-1. For example, when one discusses a concrete military task, there's no way to perform a military mission related to make life unbearable in an enclave. That's not a military sensical order. Where that language will be incorporated is more specific tasks relating to, you know, limiting convoy amounts, or tightening security in certain areas, or closing certain areas. So it's just a military -- it's just, again, more specific military language relating to how to accomplish those broader tasks, because some of the broader tasks don't lend themselves to military orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let me take you briefly back to that paragraph that talks about reducing support for UNPROFOR and the Muslim population. Would that be a section that General Tolimir would have known about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, when one looks at Directive 7-1, on, for example, page 7 of the English language one, paragraph 6(3), there is -- 6(2) and 6(3), there is specific tasks related to intelligence support and security support. General Tolimir obviously has to be aware of what those tasks are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the convoy system supporting those enclaves, was there a legitimate security element related to those that would be of interest to General Tolimir and the security branch?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those particular convoys transited through the military areas under the control of the VRS. Many parties that made up the United Nations were believed by the Republika Srpska and the VRS at the time to be hostile to the interests of the Republika Srpska. It would certainly be within the realm of the intelligence and security branch to, first of all, want to make sure that those UN forces transiting through those areas would not be collecting information or intelligence that could be used later to the detriment of the Army of the Republika Srpska. Also, it was believed by the VRS that much of the supplies that were supposedly going to civilians in the enclaves was somehow being diverted to the military forces of the Muslim side. So as a result, the VRS had a vested interest in monitoring those convoys and monitoring, in great detail, the equipment that was going in there, to take whatever steps that they believed they could take to ensure that items that could be diverted for military use against them were either eliminated from those convoys or were reduced to as small amount as possible. Obviously, some issues, like food -- food is always going to be a two-use item, so to speak. It has military and civilian applications, depending on who it's feeding. Fuel is the same way. It has both civilian and military applications. Obviously, the UN was not providing ammunition overtly to the warring parties, but those were the issues that the VRS was concerned with relating to those items which would be designated as for the civilian population but could be diverted for use by the Bosnian Muslim military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we have a situation where, as you've just testified, the VRS has a legitimate concern and responsibility to control illegal or military goods into the enclaves, on one hand, and we have what was mentioned very clearly in Directive 7, on the other hand, a policy to reduce the logistics to the UNPROFOR and the Muslim population in such a manner as to not -- as to make them dependent on their goodwill, but not condemn them in the international community, or words to that effect, if we have these two practices going on, one, the legitimate one that clearly would be a security responsibility, as you have suggested, would security know or be -- and/or be involved in the other one, the reduction as described in the Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As you lay out, this is a rather sophisticated plan that the army is attempting to pull off to achieve this objective. It's going to require a good amount of co-ordination at all levels of the intelligence and security organs and at the Main Staff in order to successfully do this without it becoming evident to the international community that it is part of a pattern of deliberate obstruction. So, yeah, given what's going to have to happen, it's going to require a great deal of support and involvement by the Main Staff organs of intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, have you had a chance over the years now to review and analyse what we refer to as convoy documents related to convoys going in and out of the various areas, such as Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us the briefest description of your understanding how this system worked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process that had to be undertaken at the actual level where the convoys were organised, put into motion to the enclaves, and then returned, required a good deal of co-ordination between the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska and the relevant organs of the UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR would be responsible for assembling a convoy and its manifested equipment that it was going to take, identifying the personnel, and then notifying the Main Staff of the VRS as to the convoy, the equipment involved, the cargo, even the names of individual soldiers and the weapons that they would be carrying, and the fuel amounts that it would be carrying. The UN had to do this in great detail. The VRS then reviewed these requests for movement and could approve them as is, could disapprove them, or could modify the cargos by directing that certain amounts be increased, decreased, whatever. Once the VRS approved these convoys, the convoy departure times and routes would be transmitted to the UN, and at the same time the various Republika Srpska military and police units that would have check-points established along the various routes and the check-points into the enclaves would be notified as to the identity of the convoy, who was travelling with the convoy, what the cargo was, how long it could remain in the enclave, and if any cargo or supplies were to be taken back, what those were. The intention, of course, from the VRS side was to not only manage the cargo being brought into the enclaves, but at a designated inspection site before entering the enclaves, they would inspect the convoy to ensure that the United Nations, in fact, complied with the approved manifest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as your review of these documents, and we'll go over some, did you form a conclusion or an opinion as to whether or not there was any restriction of logistics support reflected in these documents, consistent with or not consistent with Directive 7's language that we've talked about, reducing support to UNPROFOR and the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that as some of these convoy documents come to light, it is evident that cargo that was disapproved or restrictions placed on cargo going in made it clear that those restrictions were being done in general compliance to the goals of Directive 7, in so much as they were directed, in part, if not completely, against the civilian populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in the case of UNPROFOR, when one looks at these convoy documents, there will be many situations where the approval to move people or soldiers from the UN out of an enclave will be followed by the disapproval to allow replacement soldiers in, or to allow fuel or technical parts for vehicles into the enclaves, or to allow, for example, some weapons - you know, the explosive or propellant in the weapons expires at a certain point and the weapon needs to be replaced - you know, by not permitting those replacements to take shape. So as you look at the convoy documents, you can see the pattern which I believe falls right on track with what is outlined in Directive 7 and Directive 7-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at some of those documents. If we could go to tab 49, 65 ter 1784. And we see that this is a document, the original in the B/C/S, from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 6 March 1995. This is just a few days before the 8 March date of Directive 7, two days before, and it is to the SRK and the Drina Corps Command. And we see that it -- if we look at it, it's page 3 in the English, but we can see in the B/C/S that it is sent out by Colonel Miletic, who we know from previous evidence. And Miletic talks about -- in that first line, about UNPROFOR teams approved for 7 March 1995, and he also notes that convoys have -- there are convoys that have not been approved. And I don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but if we look through this list in the English, we'll see references in number 2 to Sarajevo, where fuel was disapproved; number 3, Gorazde, where fuel was disapproved; number 4, to Zepa, where fuel was disapproved; number 6, Sarajevo, fuel. If we go to the next page in the English, number 8, Gorazde, fuel disapproved; number 9. What do you make of these fuel disapprovals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These types of fuel disapprovals directly impact the ability of the relevant United Nations forces in the enclaves to perform their missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1784 shall be assigned Exhibit P2400. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be 2500, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to P2162. This is a document the Chamber has seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Two things I want to ask you about. We see, in this document from the Main Staff, the Army of Republika Srpska, dated 2 April, and in the text it says: "We hereby inform you that we consent to the request of the RS Co-ordinating Body ..." Can you tell us what your understanding is of the co-ordinating body that's referred to here and the interaction between it and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to civilian or humanitarian goods, the UN wasn't the only body that was dealt with in that sense. There was a civil body under the RS government, a commission, set up that would also deal with requests from the various non-governmental organisations or other humanitarian organisations that were also requesting access to the enclaves or any access to the territory of the Republika Srpska either from the Sarajevo side or from their bases in the former -- in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia out of Belgrade. So the RS commission, in and of itself, could not make unilateral approvals of these requests. They also had you reach out and go to the Main Staff of the army in order to co-ordinate these requests with the army to ensure that the army was: one, aware of the requests and, two, that they would not be approving anything that the army did not want them to approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who, in your opinion, had final control in what made it into the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a day-to-day basis, the Main Staff exercised that final approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And looking at this document, the handwritten note that we can see in the English translation is -- it says: "Not a single convoy or ICRC team or MSF may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence. M. Nikolic." Who, in your opinion, is "M. Nikolic"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be Momir Nikolic, who at the time, captain first class, was the assistant commander for Intelligence and Security for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain why Momir Nikolic would be in such a position to be able to make this statement? Is it consistent or inconsistent with what you have been telling us about, Security's involvement in these convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely consistent with the role of the security organ in monitoring the convoy movement. There was a military police check-point manned by the Bratunac Brigade at the Yellow Bridge, the entrance to the Srebrenica safe area. This was Momir Nikolic making it clear to his subordinates, in this case from a technical chain, the military police, that they were not authorised, without his personal presence there, to allow any convoy or any other vehicles into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note for the record that we have in the binder only one page and three lines of English translation. This is, in fact, the translation of the first page of the B/C/S version. The other pages are missing in the English. But could we please move to the last page of the English translation on the screen to see if there is any. That's all. That means that the other pages are missing, especially with the name of the person who is supposed to have signed it, Manojlo Milovanovic. And even in e-court, the other pages are missing in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. We did that as a resource-saver. The main thing we wanted you to see was the -- in fact, it's a convoy approval, and Momir Nikolic's comments on it, and who it is by, Milovanovic. But we can have also have this translated. It shouldn't a problem at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that was only a remark for the record, not a criticism. And, therefore, we have now put on the record that this document was signed by Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is sufficient. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to another document, 65 ter 4115, getting away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this day of trial end in keeping with God's will. I apologise to Mr. McCloskey for interrupting. I would like the Trial Chamber to be shown the whole document to see if this was ordered by Milovanovic, this order given by Nikolic. Is that the reason why not the whole document was published? Because according to the interpretation, it says that this order is in keeping with Directive 7/1. We should see whether it is, indeed, so in the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe the full document in Serbian is present in the record, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see, on the left side of the screen, the last page with the name "Manojlo Milovanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see a reference to Directive -- a specific reference to any directive here, so I'm not exactly sure what the general's concern is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you help us to understand your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I can assist you. The witness, in his reply, said that this was consistent with a directive - he literally said that on page 27 - and that these tasks were carried out by security organs. So now let's see whether that was, indeed, contained in the order, that that's how it should be done at all levels and all units, or whether Mr. Nikolic just took it upon himself to order such a thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may put a question in this respect to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in your view, did Momir Nikolic do this on his own, or do you have any indications to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure in the sense -- what you mean by "on his own." Given the guidance of Directive 7 and 7/1 to undertake a programme, in this case, the fact that Momir Nikolic is taking it upon himself to personally oversee the convoys going through and would ensure that they're complying with orders, that may be, individually, his decision. It may be a decision that Colonel Popovic, his immediate superior in the security organ, has directed. I'm not aware of any document which would indicate that one way or another. My point is that whether he's personally physically present at the convoy site or has delegated the authority to inspect these convoys and allow them to go through or not go through if their cargo is what is authorised, is part of the broader theme outlined in the various Directive 7 and 7-1. It's not an individual decision on the part of Momir Nikolic that contrary to any guidance received from anywhere else, that he, individually, will hold up international convoys going into a safe area. He does not have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think -- do you recall a document that is, I believe, in this binder where the Bratunac Brigade provides an annual report, where they talk about this topic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As part of their report that they do assessing the activities of the Bratunac Brigade, one of the issues that they note is that they are complying with orders related to monitoring UN and other international convoys going into the safe area. I believe we'll see that down the line at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to this document that we now have. We got away, briefly, from the Main Staff convoy documents. Now we're at a regular combat report from the Zvornik Brigade, dated 2 April, under the name of Vinko Pandurevic, and, of course, it's to the Drina Corps Command. And there is a section we can see on paragraph -- it's noted as paragraph 10, so we'd best go over to the next pages. Actually, we -- I guess I'm still waiting for 65 ter 4115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The reason why it took some time is that you didn't give the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We're fine in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And paragraph 10, we can see there's a section on humanitarian convoys, and it -- is this something that is normally reported on by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The daily combat reports are a reflection of the daily activities that occur within the Zvornik Brigade, or at least those activities that the command deems is necessary for the superior command, in this case the Drina Corps, to be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in the English, we can see here a reference to an UNPROFOR convoy, the Dutch Battalion, en route from Banja Koviljaca to Srebrenica. Two vehicles, four soldiers. They left at 1900 hours on 1 April. And it says: "One Veld steriliser," and it gives a number, "was seized from the Dutch Battalion." What do you make of that, a sort of sterliser being seized?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a medical device. Either it was not properly manifested or the army just decided to appropriate it for themselves and their own medical centre. They're noting, as a routine course of business, that they've done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4115 shall be assigned Exhibit P2501. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And one last document, I think, before the break, 41 -- 65 ter 4116.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is another combat report from Pandurevic dated 4 April. And it's the second page of the English that I wanted to refer you to, and that is the bottom part that talks about an MSF team going to Srebrenica, and it states that they confiscated the following from the team of MSF. And we can see it's laundry detergent, floor detergent, shampoo, towels, beer, wine, vodka, coffee, cigarettes, lighters, rolling papers. What's your comment on seizing this kind of material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A reflection, first of all, that it confirms that these convoys are being inspected, and, presumably, items that are not properly on the cargo manifest and have not been approved are being pulled off of vehicles and are being confiscated by the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On this one, can you tell whether or not this material was not -- not on the manifest or not or whether it was just being pulled?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's unclear as to the reason why this material is being pulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4116 shall be assigned Exhibit P2502 [Realtime transcript read in error "P2402"]. Thank you. Correction for the transcript. It's P2502. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I see it's 10.30, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We should have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could go, staying on the topic of convoys, to P2411. It should be in the 53 tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll -- as we get there, we'll see that we now have a main -- we're back to the Main Staff of the VRS, dated 7 April. And if we go to the end, we see this is in the name of General Milovanovic. And this is to the Command of the Drina Corps, and that we can see that this is a -- it begins as a concurrence with the co-ordinating body, and we see it sets out some of the concurrence. We also see handwritten, up in the right-hand corner, "OB." Mr. Butler, do you see -- we can see that it's been -- is a possible translation of "Security Organ." Do you make anything of "OB" written up here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the context of the electrical message or the telex going to the Command of the Drina Corps, they are being passed over to the security branch of the Drina Corps so they are aware of these convoy clearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, in that first paragraph, that: "... we concur with the implementation of permits of the Co-ordinating Body ..." Does this fit into your opinion, one way or another, about who was actually controlling these -- the final say for these, the body or the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my prior testimony, the co-ordinating body for the Republika Srpska could not, in and of themselves, authorise these movements. They would have to forward them to the Main Staff. The Main Staff would then either concur or non-concur. So, again, in this particular case, they're allowancing that, you know, they are concurring with the requests by the co-ordinating body of VRS to do this and, in effect, granting them the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise to Mr. McCloskey, but it would be good to clarify with the witness what is "approval" and what is "authorisation," because the two words have been used. And, second, to see whether the security organs received this telegram or what we see up above are the initials of someone to who it is addressed, because it doesn't say "Security Organs" at the top, it says "The Drina Corps." Where can Mr. McCloskey show us that it was sent to the security organs of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I stand by Mr. Butler's answer to the questions. This is the evidence. There is a reflection of "OB/Security Organ" on this, and it is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should take notice of the fact that nobody suggested that this typewritten document was sent to a security organ, and Mr. McCloskey dealt with a handwritten entry. Mr. Tolimir asked you, Mr. McCloskey, to discuss the words "approval" and "authorisation." If you would do that at this point in time, that's fine. Otherwise, Mr. Tolimir may do that during his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. Butler, could you just reiterate what -- which, if either term, is more appropriate for the Main Staff's action or authority? Are they approving, or are they authorising, or are they both, or are they neither?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I don't split the two terms up, "approving" and "authorising." The -- under the methodology used with respect to convoys, it was the responsibility of other organs to propose which convoys would travel and what their cargo are, and ultimately it was the responsibility of the Main Staff to approve those requests. Now, whether one calls them "approval" or whether one calls them "we concur with that request," in my understanding of the phraseology, it's the same thing. The ultimate authority as to whether or not a convoy travels is vested with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you something. We see that -- on that first page, for example, we see that it's approved to send flour both to Gorazde and to Srebrenica, and I think it has been shown or mentioned in this case that there's a video of ammunition being pulled out of flour on one of the convoys to I can't recall which enclave. Would the security branch be concerned about ammunition going to the enclaves inside flour, as apparently occurred based on a video that is believed part of this record?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would be absolutely prudent for them to inspect even those types of cargos to ensure that elements of the UN or ABiH had not gotten access to those goods and had sought to smuggle in weapons. So the fact, particularly, that the VRS had evidence that it occurred in the past is a good indicator that they should continue to look for evidence of that and inspect the cargos in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't want to be repetitive, but to make sure General Tolimir understands your opinion: Given, as you've just said, there is a legitimate security concern for the security branch to control what goes in these convoys, is it militarily possible or practical that the security branch would be cut out of a system that actually restricted humanitarian and support for UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. They would have to be involved in the process in order to perform that duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Couldn't General Mladic or Milovanovic appoint a special task force to be involved in the restrictions of -- the illegal restrictions of convoys that was totally separate and apart from the legitimate controlling and restrictions of illegal goods? Is that imaginable in a military context?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to ask, could we have a reference? Where are security organs controlling convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is part of the process of the evidence, and Mr. Butler has talked at length about it already. And I think that's a good point for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We agree. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember my question, Mr. Butler? It basically comes down to: Can you have security involved in this legitimate control of material and have some other -- complete other unit acting -- doing the same fundamental thing, but illegally restricting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic or Milovanovic could organise it, obviously, any way that they elect to, but it doesn't make sense that you would have two separate organs essentially involved in the same act, which is dealing with the issues of cargo, and the inspection of that cargo, and the dealing of convoys. It seems to be -- it seems to be repetitive. And given the fact that the security organ, you know, has an ability to accomplish these missions, it would make sense for them just to allow them to do both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise for objecting again, but it says here -- or, rather, in the question just asked by Mr. McCloskey on page 37, line 5, he says, Can you have security involved in control? Can we get a reference where exactly are security involved in the control of convoys? And then he goes on to say that Milovanovic and others could organise it, and the witness answered that question, but we need to see first where exactly and how the security organs controlled the convoys. I want to establish the facts. Maybe the question could be rephrased to sound something like, Can we suppose that security organs, and so on and so forth, but we need to establish the facts. We need to stick to facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the Prosecution is trying to establish facts. It's their examination of the witness, and later on it's your turn to cross-examine the witness. This is not a real objection, and there's no foundation for this objection to the last question, which is already answered. Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, untruths are being presented here, and you approve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I ruled on that. The witness has given his answers, and Mr. McCloskey may continue. Please don't interrupt in that way. If that is in your opinion, and this is -- you are absolutely entitled to see it as untruths, you should and you have the opportunity for that, to challenge this part of the examination-in-chief during your cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just to remind us all, Captain First Class Momir Nikolic, when he made the comment that we saw on the convoy document, was -- in what capacity do you believe he was acting when he made that comment about no convoys would go through without his approval?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made that comment in his capacity as his role as chief of security for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. He's exercising his authority, as it's been delegated to him, to ensure that the contents of those convoys contain no more cargo than is authorised on the manifest. So, I mean, maybe I'm not saying it as clearly as I need to with respect to control, but, I mean, at that point at that Yellow Bridge, at that point where the convoy goes into UN territory, Captain Nikolic is exercising control over that convoy. If he were to find material that was not in compliance, he would be within his authority, as granted to him by the Main Staff, to inform the Main Staff that the convoy does not contain material as manifested and leave it up to the Main Staff as to whether or not that convoy should continue to go forth, or whether or not that convoy will be turned around, or, as we saw in the case of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, whether or not the material that was not on the manifest would be off-loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- we should be on page -- are we on page 2? Yes, we are, of the English. And the B/C/S may be the next page. The important part that I want to go for is a comment that says "Remark," and: "We did not approve the following in this weekly plan." So we started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is still on the first page of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We started with an approval that we've noted, and now we're seeing material that is not approved. And it says: "Material for the Swedish construction project for Srebrenica and Drinjaca on 9 April, 11 April and 13 April for Srebrenica, until we receive the position of the state committee for co-operation regarding this matter." Can you remind us what this Swedish construction project is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's often referred to in documents as the Swedish shelter project as well. It was an NGO programme where this particular group was constructing temporary housing for those individuals residing both inside the Srebrenica area as well as Bosnian Serbs who had been displaced outside, temporary housing, rather than -- because they were refugees. So, I mean, this NGO was involved in that project of the construction of temporary housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says: "In addition to the above, we did not approve beef, salt, oil and clapboards for the enclave ..." And it gives several dates. These basic foodstuffs, salt, oil, beef, was hunger an issue in the enclave in the summer, in June and July of 1995 for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand that as a result of the investigation, there were a number of issues that were raised with the fact that the food stocks within the enclave were at dangerously low levels as the year was wearing on because the food products weren't being brought in as fast as they were being consumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's your understanding of this term "clapboards"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it at this juncture we're talking about drywall, construction material type of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, all right, and that is already in evidence. Let's now go to 65 ter 1925. This is also a document from 7 April, and we see again it's from the Main Staff, in the name of General Milovanovic, and we again -- if we see the Serbian, we see "OB" up in the right-hand corner. Again, tell us what's your understanding of what "OB" stands for.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notation for "OB" would define as "Security Organ."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your view, the fact that someone would write "Security Organ" on this document, does that have any meaning to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, while, obviously, the compliance of all orders is with respect to, you know, the role of the commander, in these particular cases monitoring convoy movements and ensuring compliance would be a security function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's just see this. We see that this really -- this starts out as a document where they have not approved several UNPROFOR convoys and teams. And I won't go over it all in detail, but number 1, we see to Sarajevo, fuel; Sarajevo, diesel, number 2; number 3, Gorazde, fuel, kerosene, unleaded fuel and gas; number 4, Sarajevo, and it talks about 27 vehicles and 63 persons which was supposed to transport 12 containers with humanitarian aid, bed, food, clothes, medicines, and school supplies. If we go to page 2 in the English, still on B/C/S page 1, I believe, it talks about more Sarajevo material, oil, solvents, maintenance supply, and it says: "In view of the fact that UNPROFOR did not deliver a drop of the agreed 13.000 litres of oil for the winter season for road maintenance work in winter, we demanded that they fulfill their obligation and said that we would then discuss approving oil for their needs." What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, as part of the various access agreements, one of the agreements made was that UNPROFOR would provide fuel to -- or oils to the Republika Srpska which, in their view, would be used, in part, in order to keep the roads clear for UN convoys as well their own traffic. In this particular document, it reflects the fact that their view is that none of the promised oil supplies from the UN have been delivered to the Republika Srpska, and, as a result, they're going to retaliate by cutting the supply of fuels going to the UN until such time as the UN makes good on their promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we continue to go down, we see that number 9, Srebrenica, on April 8th, a convoy compromising seven vehicles and eighteen persons which were supposed to transport diesel fuel, it got denied. And according to this paragraph, Milovanovic says: "We told them that they had 79 tonnes of fuel with Oric." What does that mean, that last comment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naser Oric is the commander of the 28th Infantry Division inside the Srebrenica enclave. This is a rather flippant remark that the Main Staff is making to their Drina Corps counterparts which essentially is telling them that from their perspective, they're not approving fuel going into the enclave because the military forces of the ABiH already have more than enough fuel, and they're not going to provide them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any indication that the BiH had such amounts of fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly hold open the possibility that the ABiH, and specifically the 28th Infantry Division, was seeking to divert fuel going to either UNPROFOR or to civilians in Srebrenica for military use, but I've not come across anything which reflects that at any given time they had this much fuel on hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you aware of any military vehicles they had that would use fuel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th Infantry Division was primarily light infantry because they did not have very many vehicles. They couldn't, under the demilitarisation, actually be driving vehicles back and forth in front of the Dutch, so in this particular context, just not a military use. I suspect that if the 28th Military Division was using fuel in these quantities, it was primarily for the purpose of selling it on the black market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would be the consumer in Srebrenica for 28th Division fuel black market, if there was such a thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian population would be the primary consumer. It certainly wouldn't be unheard of to find out that some elements of the 28th Infantry Division might have even been selling fuel back to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at paragraph 10. This is page 3 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Mindua would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. In fact, I wanted to put a question now because I thought that the Prosecutor wanted to get to the next document. But, nevertheless, since I was given the floor, I will put a question now. So, Mr. Witness, you just talked about the black market. And if I look at the document that I have before me, 1925, paragraph 4, General Milovanovic says the following: He's, in fact, not authorising the passage of convoys, number 07-181/04, because the activities by the UNPROFOR are already carried out by a great number of international organisations, or NGOs, actually. So according to him, according to General Milovanovic, the UNPROFOR is supposed to take care or carry out tasks within its mandate. So here we see that the UNPROFOR, or at least when it comes to the convoy we're talking about, was composed of 12 containers with humanitarian aid, beds, food, clothes, medicines, and school supplies. So could you please tell us: How do you explain this attitude by General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the document, it reflects that their view, particularly in Srebrenica, you know, what they believed to be the limited mandate of the United Nations forces there, the Dutch Battalion forces, which were to essentially maintain the boundaries, as undefined as they were, of the Srebrenica enclave and to enforce the demilitarisation of the 28th Infantry Division inside the enclave, not necessarily that it was the UNPROFOR's job to maintain and support the civilian population. That's about as much as I can read into that particular comment. I mean, obviously General Milovanovic would be a better source of information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. I understand, in fact, because the problem, in fact, is the following, and this is what the Prosecutor is seeking to establish: is that the VRS was attempting to block various convoys in order to create an impact on the Muslim population, and here we have General Milovanovic who's supporting something else or who says something else, so this is why I wanted to get your opinion. But according to you, only General Milovanovic can explain his own thoughts. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the sense that General Milovanovic is the best to explain his own thoughts. What I would reiterate again for you, sir, is that as part of the plan that the VRS is undertaking, it wasn't just enough to restrict the flow of goods going into the enclaves. As articulated in Directive 7 and 7/1, it had to be done in such a manner that the Republika Srpska would not be unduly criticised in the way that they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one last paragraph in this document, paragraph 10, and this is a convoy that was refused to Srebrenica, comprising 13 vehicles and 24 persons, which were supposed to transport various goods; a water trailer, a large quantity of field beds, hospital beds, an X-ray machine, beams for construction, nails, light fittings, a satellite telephone system and cables, signalling equipment, roofing material, office supplies, and cleaning goods. In your understanding, Mr. Butler, did UNPROFOR share their medical abilities with -- by helping provide medical treatment for the Muslims of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that a number of the Dutch medical personnel, who've testified, I'm not sure in this trial but certainly in other trials, have indicated that they often shared their medical supplies and support and treated the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1925 shall be assigned Exhibit P2503. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to temporarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me, but I cannot help noticing, on page 44, line 7, where Judge Mindua asked the question, and the witness's answer begins with line 23 and straddles page 45, I think there was a slight misunderstanding because the number mentioned by Judge Mindua relates to the convoy from Kiseljak to Sarajevo, and the witness's answer makes it looks like it was related to Srebrenica, because he also mentioned the 28th Division. I believe it would be good to have a clear record on this issue, because Judge Mindua, on page 44, line 14, mentioned Convoy 07-181/4, and the document says this convoy was supposed to go from Kiseljak to Sarajevo on the 8th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a correct statement. Number 4 in this document -- or item number 4 is related to a convoy from Kiseljak to Sarajevo. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, to me, it was very clear that General Mindua was -- excuse me, His Honour Judge Mindua --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He's not a military judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- was referring to the Srebrenica section, where General Milovanovic had made the remarks that he didn't feel that this humanitarian material was part of the mandate.
