I think that was very clear on the record. If there was a mistake in the reference, I think we can all -- we all remember what the question was about, and I think it was very clear. So I prefer not to go back there, unless someone thinks it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have the different views on the record. Everybody is able to check the document, itself. You may continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now I would like to temporarily go past many of these documents and save them for the end, and go now to tab 60, which is 65 ter 1933. And we see that this is a -- from the Main Staff, dated 22 April. It's to the Command of Military Post 7111. Mr. Butler, do you remember which military post that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military Post 7111 should be the Command of the Drina Corps, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we note that this says: "We wish to inform you that we have approved the travel of the following UNPROFOR convoys and teams:" And then it lists that under number 1. And then it goes on to say: "At the same time, we wish to inform you that we have not approved travel of the following convoys." And then we see, on the English, number 1 is a Sarajevo convoy for fuel. Then we need to turn the page, and we see a long list of convoy disapprovals for -- as we take a look at this, we see that there's Sarajevo for fuel - I won't read them all out - Gorazde, Gorazde, Gorazde, Zepa regarding the transfer of UN VP from Zepa. What do you take "VP" to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "VP" in this context is "Military Police."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's from General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to -- and if we note -- try to remember the numbers that we're seeing here, "23-309/04" is the first, and then we see "23-331/04," in sequence. If we go to the next document under tab 61, we see the Main Staff is sending this to UNPROFOR. The last one went to the Drina Corps, and we see some of the same numbers. The first ones that have not been approved is "23-309/04," and describes various -- and it's a list. And I want to go over Convoy 1, Convoy 6 and Convoy 10, which we will find as we go through the B/C/S. So if we could first go -- it should be page 3 of the English, page 2 of the B/C/S. And this should be, if I didn't say it - I'm sorry, it may have been the problem - 65 ter 5243. I apologise. That was covered up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S, page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we -- this is number 23-309/04, which was number 1 on the first page which was not approved. And for this question, Mr. Butler, I will tell you that the top of the B/C/S page, where we see in Cyrillic "ne" or "no," and initials, it's the Prosecution's position that those initials are those initials for General Tolimir. So in this particular document, we see that fuel is being disapproved. If the Prosecution is correct and these are, in fact, General Tolimir's initials with a "ne" next to it, would this -- his involvement in the approval or disapproval of convoys be consistent with his position as chief of Intel and Security?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to Convoy 6, which should be page 7 of the B/C/S, page 13. This is number 23-349/04, which is another document, Kiseljak to Gorazde, that was refused. And we can see what the request was that was refused; the British convoy, supplies for the British soldiers. And if we look at the B/C/S, we see "ne" up at the top written in, and it's the position of the Prosecution that those initials that look something like a coat hanger are those of General Tolimir. And as we look down at the B/C/S, we see various comments and "ne" written throughout that document. And if we turn the page in the English, we get the translation's effort to reproduce those "ne"s, and we can see the materials here; tools, wire, 11.000 litres of packed water, a music system. Would this be consistent with General Tolimir's position, as chief of Intel and Security, in your view ? Why would a general be involved in disapproving such a -- such a request, or, excuse me, proposing a disapproval?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the document is a reflection of the importance that was placed on the monitoring of materials going into various enclaves that the Main Staff placed upon itself, that they paid very close attention to detail. Each individual item was examined with respect to where -- whether or not it was justified to be on the manifest, in their view. And as you'll note, in some cases where even requests are approved, amounts might be reduced. So, again, I believe this is a reflection of how important this particular job was within the Main Staff and that General Tolimir is personally involved in the monitoring of the cargo that is potentially going into these enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has seen evidence of these convoy requests with the initials. Witnesses have testified identifying the initials of Ratko Mladic on them, I think General Milan Gvero, and others. Would it be consistent for other senior members of the Main Staff, including General Mladic, himself, to be involved in this -- in this process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Given the gravity of the situation as it was approached by the Main Staff, the fact that other senior members of the Main Staff are taking a hands-on approach to this would be consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to number -- which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we for a moment stay with this document, please. I would like to put a question to Mr. Butler, and I would like to ask him to make some markings on this, with the assistance of the Court Usher. Mr. McCloskey referred to some handwritten parts of this document. We see, in the top, the "ne," and then a slash, and then some handwritten markings. Could you please indicate which part of these handwritten marks you suppose that they are from General Tolimir? Please encircle these parts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. I understand that that particular set of initials the investigation has attributed to General Tolimir. Those are the only comments that I can personally attribute to. I note that -- the writing here, the "no," and that is consistent, but I don't know General Tolimir's handwriting to any degree necessary to be able to conclude that those individual comments are, in fact, his handwritten comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know, if at all, that these initials on top of that page are from Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, sir, my understanding of whom that signature comes to is derived from the work of the investigation, that they have sourced that through a variety of methods. I don't have personal knowledge that that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation. Mr. McCloskey, are you tendering this marked map --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- to have a consistent record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked page will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, e-court page 7 of the 65 ter document 5243 shall be assigned Exhibit P2504. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And my question was -- it was the position of the Prosecution that that was the initials, and that's the reason why I did that. And I would refer you to the testimony of General Milovanovic, who you may recall identified initials. I don't think he identified this particular page, but he -- you will recall him identifying that General Tolimir had two sets of initials, Cyrillic and Latin. All right. Then if we could -- I believe we need to now go to number 10 on this initial list, which is number 23/03 on the Serbian document, and that should be B/C/S page 11 and page 21 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we know to refer you back to the front page of 5243 that this is one of the numbers that was disapproved by the VRS. And again, Mr. Butler, if we look at this, we see that this is a request from -- or to the Main Staff, from Nicolai - if we go to the second page on the English - requesting this, which was disapproved. Number 1 was the movement from Sarajevo to Zepa. The journey will take place en route from Sarajevo via Pale. The purpose of the movement was to transfer to Zepa. And then it identifies the persons that are travelling in this movement as UN military observers. So can you just tell us what this is, and is it consistent or inconsistent with any knowledge you had of what was going on at Srebrenica related to military observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is consistent with the overall plan to reduce the effectiveness of UN military monitors and observers, in part, by not allowing personnel replacement of observers who finished their tour of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And like you did the last one, could you circle -- and, again, it's the Prosecution's position that we see the initials next to the "ne" up in the top. Can you circle what you have learned from the investigation to be, according to the investigation, the initials of General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now could I offer that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked page will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, B/C/S page 11 in e-court of the 65 ter 5243, marked by the witness in court, shall be assigned Exhibit P2505. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to be consistent, let's go to the first document. It should be page 2 in the B/C/S, page 3 in the English, I believe. I'm not good at going backwards, but I think we've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for this, can you circle what you have learned the investigation has identified as General Tolimir's initials?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This marked page will be received as an exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, B/C/S page 2 of the 65 ter 5243, marked by the witness in court, shall be assigned Exhibit P2506. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer the whole exhibit, 65 ter 5243, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5243 shall be assigned Exhibit P2507. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, and what about 65 ter 1933?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Apparently I've forgotten one of the documents that we've just spoken to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just asked you. What about 65 ter 1933?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Stewart got me at the same time. I apologise. I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1933 shall be assigned Exhibit P2508. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go forward but -- and I will continue to discuss with Mr. Gajic the possibility of saving some time with these documents. But he has very fairly said to me that he thought it was important for each of the documents to be seen and commented by Butler, so it is my intention to come back. But it's a time-consuming effort, so I'd like to get on with the chronology and come back to the convoy documents, if that's necessary. So I'd like to skip ahead to tab 70, and it's P2167.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting for that to come up: We'll see that it's from the Command of the Bratunac Brigade on the 4th of July, 1995, and it's entitled "Analysis of combat readiness in the first half of 1995," and it's delivered to the Drina Corps, and it's in the name of Commander Colonel Blagojevic. Now, this is -- we've seen combat readiness reports from the Main Staff, from the Drina Corps. Is this similar to those in some way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But rather than in this context of being an annual evaluation, this particular report is a semi-annual evaluation, covering the first six months of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to page 16 in the English and page 29 in the B/C/S. And we can see that this is the chapter on intelligence and security support, and would Momir Nikolic have played a role in the drafting of this section of the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Given that it relates to intelligence and security support, I would expect that he would be the primary drafter of this particular section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't go through all of it, but as we see six paragraphs down from the top, there's a mention of intelligence data is collected through reconnaissance of combat dispositions by reconnaissance squads, interrogations of prisoners of war, and surveillance of forward positions. So would the security support, under the rules and practices, as you've talked about, include interrogation of prisoners of war, as noted here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: More under the intelligence function of it, but generally as part of the intelligence and security branch, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it also -- the last paragraph on the English talks about: "The Military Police Platoon has been engaged as planned on the orders of the brigade commander. Training was also planned and completed in accordance with the possibilities and appropriately to the situation." So now here is -- we have a section under the intel and security support of the mention of the military police, and its use and training, on orders of the brigade commander. Can you just wrap that up for us a bit and -- it's something that we've heard a lot of, but how does the brigade commander and the security support connect into the command structure of the military police, and based on this practical application that we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The application in this document, how it was, again, practically applied reflects how it was envisioned under the broader regulations that were published under the SFRY with respect to their regulations on the military police, their use and functions. The police, as part of that organisational formation, are ultimately subordinate to and responsible to the commander of that unit; in this case, the brigade commander. However, it is the security officer who is responsible for proposing methods of training, the employment of the use of the police, and all of those other associated technical issues, one, to the commander for his approval, and subsequent to the commander's approval, carrying them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "subsequent to the commander's approval, carrying them out," what are you saying is the responsibilities of the security officer, vis-a-vis the military police, in carrying out the commander's orders, just specifically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- after the commander approves a proposal, the security officer or, in fact, across the staff, any officer at any of those technical services, you know, is going to issue supplemental orders in order to more concretely define the tasks that have to be done and how those will be accomplished. He is doing so -- he is giving those orders as a security officer, but he's doing so in light of the orders that he has received from the commander. So in a practical sense, where you will have instances of Momir Nikolic, for example, giving orders directly to the military police, you know, in the competent performance of his duties, he is giving those orders in the light of the guidance and directions he has received from his superiors, in this particular case related to training and implementation of the military police, from the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do the rules envisage him receiving directives from his superior in the security chain or branch; in this case, Vujadin Popovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where would Vujadin Popovic be getting his orders from along the command chain?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the command chain, Vujadin Popovic would be receiving his orders from the Drina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the evening of 13 July and afterward, who would that have been?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 2000 hours onwards on 13 July 1995, his commander would have been General Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for Popovic, aside from his commander, Krstic, could he be receiving, under the rules, directives and instructions from his superior along the security branch chain, Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was Ljubisa Beara's direct supervisor and superior?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: July of 1995, that would have been General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to page -- it should be 17 of this same document. We're still under the "Intelligence and Security Support" section. It should be page 31 of the B/C/S, and I hope this will help General Tolimir in the question he had earlier. This says: "In the brigade's area of responsibility, a check-point was established for the control of all international organisations entering and leaving the enclave of Srebrenica. This check-point functions in accordance with the orders of the Main Staff of the VRS and instructions and orders of the brigade commander." Now, does this paragraph suggest in any way to you that there is any intel or security involvement in the control of the check-point?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the lowest level, the check-point is manned by the military police, again, under the command of the brigade commander, but, from a technical perspective, answerable to the security officer as to how they conduct their activities. This particular paragraph is a good reflection of how that works.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see this paragraph is under the section of "Intelligence and Security Support." Could it have been anywhere or, in your view, is it under this section for a reason?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's under this section because it belongs here, because these are classical duties and responsibilities of these types of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And taking us back to that document that we recall, a convoy approval, where there's a note where Momir Nikolic says, No MSF can go in without my approval, something to that effect, how does that fit into this brigade report and your conclusion you've just given us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's consistent with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now we're going to change gears a bit and go away from convoys and their control, back to the narrative of -- where you have identified various documents occurring and the chronology as we go towards July 1995. And the first one I'd like to take you to is tab 71. It's 65 ter 2094. And as we're waiting for that, I will note that this is from the Drina Corps Command. It's a regular combat report identified as "Urgent." If we go to the last page in English, we don't need to for these purposes, but we'll see it's under the name of Deputy Commander Colonel Radislav Krstic. And I don't want to go into all the detail of it, but I do want to ask you about this one reference under paragraph 2: "We are continuing with preparations for stabilisation of defence around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, in accordance with your order. We are currently unable to implement your order to fully close off the enclaves and carry out attacks against them because we do not have sufficient forces ..." Then it goes on. Now, we see that this regular combat report is to the RS and the forward command post of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, so can you tell us, in a nutshell, what you believe Colonel Krstic at this point is telling the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular segment of the report, Colonel Krstic is alluding to the fact that they've been given previously orders to fully close off the enclaves, and he's informing them that based on the current situation, and specifically the fact that they do not have enough resources, military units in this particular context, that they're unable to comply with that particular mission. But what they are attempting to do is to still interdict, at least sporadically, those lines of communication back and forth and attack those enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. This reference to "your order to fully close off the enclaves" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I see Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't see it. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies to Mr. McCloskey, but could he explain where it is that mention is made in this document of "Muslim forces attack"? Can that be cleared with the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the general's asked you to explain what you meant by your last -- I think the last comment, that you said that -- something about the Drina Corps was continuing to attack the enemy.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reading back my last answer, and that's -- I don't think I said "Muslim forces attack." My last answer was that in this particular segment of the report, Colonel Krstic is alluding to the fact that they've been given an order previously to close off the enclave, and he is informing them, based on the current situation, he does not have enough resources or military units to complete that mission. And then the next thing I said was what they are attempting to do is to still interdict, at least sporadically, those lines of communication back and forth and attack those enemy forces. And where I derive that from is the line in paragraph 2 of the document, which specifically says: "... but we are continuing to take specific measures to uncover enemy groups in the gap ..." The presumption that I have being if they are able to identify those groups infiltrating back and forth into Srebrenica, between Srebrenica and Zepa, that once identified, if they have the ability, they will attack them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And back to my question. This language there that says that they're unable to implement the Main Staff order to -- well, that's my language. What I want to ask you about is: This language about "fully close off the enclaves," that particular language, do you tie that in or relate that to anything from Directive 7 or some other documents previous to this that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's those tasks or those tasks articulated in Directive 7 or 7/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the wording -- I don't want to go back to those, but do you roughly remember the wording of Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it specifically said to ensure the physical separation of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 2094 shall be assigned Exhibit P2509. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good stopping time, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We must have our second break now, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we left off with this document where Colonel Krstic tells the Main Staff they're unable to attack Srebrenica and Zepa. It was on 16 May. I'll jump ahead a bit, but at some point later on did the Drina Corps -- was the Drina Corps able to gear up for an attack on the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By the end of May of 1995, the Drina Corps did undertake a limited military operation against the enclave, particularly the military operation related to the capture of what's known as UN Observation Post Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get to that momentarily, but I want to get to another document that relates to some prisoners and the intel branch. So could we go to P2140. It should be 72 tab. And we see -- I hope people have a better B/C/S version. I know it's a very bad version all the way around. But we see that this is from the VRS Main Staff, Intelligence and Security Sector. That's General Tolimir's sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's in the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember who he was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer on the Main Staff. He worked in the Intelligence Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And this is entitled "NATO air-strikes," and it talks about: "We have information that the NATO session was finished on 27 May at around 1600 hours, and it was decided that massive NATO air-strikes against VRS positions and features would continue." It talks a bit more about that and where they believe that the attacks will occur; on ammunition dumps, fire positions, anti-aircraft defence equipment, artillery, and such. And it says, the last line: "Familiarise commanders with this information and recommend that captured members of UN forces be placed in an area of a possible NATO air-strike." What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, towards the end of May of 1995, related to issues around Sarajevo, NATO launched a series of air-strikes against military positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, primarily fixed positions, ammunition bunkers, communications facilities. In retaliation to these attacks by NATO, the VRS, where they had the opportunity to do so, took members of UN military forces into custody. What this particular last line of the paragraph reflects is that those individuals who are captured should be placed at facilities or installations which they believe will be targets of attack. I'm aware that there is video footage that exists which, in fact, shows members of UN forces, restrained by handcuffs or other means, at VRS military installations, and that those videos were publicised as a way to convince NATO to not bomb those particular facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can we try to blow up the B/C/S, where we have the signature block? It's to the left of the stamp. Not the stamp, the -- yeah. Maybe one more time, because we have an English translation that says: "On the authorisation of the chief," and then: "Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion on who the chief is in this sentence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe in this context, the head of the sector, which is General Tolimir, he is the assistant commander for Intelligence and Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could this be Mladic as well, the chief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall ever seeing any written document, the context of "the chief" and being General Mladic. In Main Staff documents of that nature, I would more likely attribute the phrase, if it's from the Main Staff directly, "the chief" to be General Milovanovic. So I've never seen General Mladic associated with the phrase "the chief."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this document reflect work that would be associated with intel and security work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The fact that it's talking about the receipt of strategic intelligence, that information they have received from the NATO session, and that the decision has been made that NATO will continue air-strikes on the VRS. And the second paragraph, an intelligence assessment of what the potential targets are in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captured members of the UN forces would, presumably, be handled along the same measures that they would handle other detainees or prisoners of war, which, as you're aware, did fall under the purview, to some degree, of the Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document. It's 65 ter 3277. This on the same subject. It's from the Main Staff, "Very Urgent," to the command of various corps, including the Drina Corps, entitled "The reception and deployment of the UNPROFOR members in the corps area of responsibility." This is in the name of the deputy commander, Lieutenant General Milovanovic, and he is ordering -- we see in number 1: "I hereby order corps commands and the VIPVO --" Can you tell us what "VIPVO" is, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be Air and Anti-Aircraft Defence Forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. "... shall in agreement with commanders of the logistics bases place the captured UNPROFOR staff, as well as the staff of other international humanitarian organisations, in their areas of responsibility ..." And it talks about various places. And if we go to the next page in English under paragraph 4 it mentions: "The Command of the Drina Corps shall place the captured UNPROFOR troops and members of the other humanitarian organisations at the installations in its area of responsibility." Do you in any way relate this order by General Milovanovic on the 27th of May with this document by Karanovic that was made, according to him, on the authorisation of the chief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, they are related documents. The first document reflects the proposal. The second document reflects the command of the VRS acting on that proposal and, in effect, adopting that proposal and issuing implementing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we see this document that we're looking at now in the name of Deputy Commander Milovanovic, but the Court has learned, as I'm sure General Tolimir will agree with me, that his title is chief of staff/deputy commander. So going back to the Karanovic document, and it says: "On authorisation of the chief," could this be Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the first document where the phrase is "Chief"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that Karanovic writes up.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it is, sir, no. And one of the reasons why that I think is relevant is if you were to look back at that particular document, which is P2140, and look who originated it, it comes from the Intelligence and Security Sector and it has their coding number on it, 12/45-596. So it is a document originated by the Intelligence and Security Sector. Their chief is not General Milovanovic. Their chief is General Tolimir. The second document is not -- which is, I guess, what, Papa 3277, the second document is not originated by the Intelligence staff. It's directed -- it's issued by the Main Staff, their operative branch, and it has the number 03-4. And, of course, on this particular day, they're both dated the same day, and General Milovanovic is identifying himself specifically on that day as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In any event, Karanovic's document, P2140, would General Tolimir, in your view, be fully aware of this document and approve its content?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, given the gravity of this particular situation, where they are taking UN personnel hostage, they're involved in being bombed by NATO forces, General Tolimir should very much be involved in at least knowing what is in this document and what the ramifications of it are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer 65 ter 3277 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 3277 shall be assigned Exhibit P2510. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to tab 74. It should be 65 ter 3981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, Sector for Intelligence and Security, 13 February 1995, to the East Bosnia Corps, the Drina Corps, and to the chief of the Intelligence and Security Department of the East Bosnia Corps by messenger, the chief of the Security and Intelligence Department, the Drina Corps, by messenger, and the Krajina Corps Command. It's called "Demarcating the front-line, instructions." And if we go to the last page, page 4 of the English, which we don't need to as yet, we'll see that this is in the name of Assistant Commander Major General Zdravko Tolimir, and we'll see his initials, "ZT," under the document. Just looking at the first page of this document, we see that it starts out with: "The Drina Corps Command will not mark the front-line around the Muslim enclaves in Zepa and Srebrenica, since these enclaves have been marked and defined with the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica." And then it says: "You are to explain to the representatives of UNPROFOR and the Muslim forces in the ZRK that the status of Zepa and Srebrenica will be resolved in accordance with the agreements on their demilitarisation." It goes on and talks about that a bit and then makes references to a hamlet, Podraveno [phoen], and a village with a trig point. And he says: "In addition, it is unclear who is in control of the Zeleni Jadar factory, considering its significance and the fact that only the UNPROFOR check-point is located inside it and that the Muslim forces are approximately one kilometre away from the factory ..." Now, you had just mentioned Zeleni Jadar as an important location. Does this reference by General Tolimir have anything to do with what you were talking about, in terms of the strategic location, or is this the same place or something different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same place, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when the general says "considering its significance," what do you believe that means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one looks at the terrain in and around the Srebrenica enclave, and the logical routes by which an attacking force can get to Srebrenica, perhaps the most important one, from the Bosnian Serb military perspective, was the road leading from the south through Zeleni Jadar and then onwards to Srebrenica. In early January 1995, then Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic, had actually made a comment to UN observers that he had at the Drina Corps, that they would know when the Serbs were ready to take Srebrenica, because the first thing that they would do is take Zeleni Jadar. When one looks at the military operations in 1993 against Srebrenica before the enclave was established, the main axis of attack came through that route. And if one looks at how the main military attack occurred in July of 1995, you will again note that the main axis of attack came through that particular area. So the Bosnian Serb military was well aware that controlling Zeleni Jadar was an important precursor to the ability to launch a military operation against Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so does General Tolimir note what the problem is regarding Zeleni Jadar here, or as he describes the location, does he identify what units are there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular document, what he's referencing is the fact that apparently, according to the map graphics that were forwarded, it's not clear to the Main Staff who's actually controlling the facility or the town of Zeleni Jadar. He notes that they have the UN check-point there, but that the lines seem to reflect the fact that the Muslims don't control the town, certainly the Serbs don't control the town, so, again, this is his response back to the Drina Corps saying, in a sense, that, The graphics that you have sent me are not accurate, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then as we look at this document on the next page in English, I just note that as you look through it, talking about the -- as he talks about the area and the demarcation lines, there is an amazing amount of detail. There's trig points, there's villages, there's streams, elevations. And if we go to the next page, page 3, similar amazing detail. And this is actually drafted by General Tolimir. What, if anything, can you say about the amount of detailed knowledge that is going into this document from General Tolimir for such a small place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, if one assumes that General Tolimir, personally, did not spend hours parsing over these things and that one of his subordinates did, it certainly reflects the fact that these graphics, when they came in from the corps to the Main Staff, someone paid a great deal of attention to them to make sure that they were very accurate. General Tolimir was made aware of this long laundry list of inaccuracies in the lines and felt it was of enough significance to send a response back to the Drina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps, requesting that they send more accurate graphics or positions to more accurately reflect where the front-lines are and who's in control of what particular points of territory. So it does -- it reflects an amazing attention to detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On whose part?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If not General Tolimir, certainly his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about General Tolimir? Does this show that he has an attention to detail, or can you separate him from the document in some way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't separate from -- him from the document, in the sense that he has signed it and he is sending it forward. The whole reason why a military -- or that staff officers exist to support their superior commanders is because it is recognised that commanders don't have time to handle everything personally. So, again, I mean, I don't exclude the possibility that General Tolimir, personally, spent the necessary time to come up with this type of detail, but I think it's more likely that one of his subordinate staff officers was directed to do so by him, came up with this particular response, and when General Tolimir was appraised on the large number of inaccuracies, he took it upon himself to then go back to the Drina Corps and East Bosnia Corps and request clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 3981 shall be assigned Exhibit P2511. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we now go to P625. This is a document the Trial Chamber has seen more than once. It is from the Command of the Drina Corps, Forward Command Post Pribicevac, dated 2 June 1995, entitled "Restoration of the control over the facilities and the Zeleni Jadar asphalt road," and it's an order in the name, as we can see from page 2 of the English and of the B/C/S, that it's the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it starts out: "Considering, from the military/security aspect, that the conditions have been created for the entry into Zeleni Jadar industrial facilities ..." And it goes on and describes the background, and then it gives an order that we're familiar with about taking down the UN OP that is there. Is -- does this relate to the area of Zeleni Jadar that you were talking about previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what does this indicate? And I don't mean the particulars of it. We've all seen how they -- what the recommendation is on how Legenda and the troops are to act. But what does this indicate is going on at this time or planned to go on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, in general, indicates how the Drina Corps Command expects elements of the Bratunac Brigade and the Drina Corps Manoeuvre Battalion, in this case the Drina Wolves, to successfully capture the town, and how to successfully neutralise the United Nations' check-point there using as little violence and risk of casualties to the UN as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, in your view, is the overall objective to taking control of this area at this time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective is to take control of Zeleni Jadar, again with the knowledge that controlling Zeleni Jadar is a precursor to launching larger operations against Srebrenica. Was that in the mind of the two lieutenants or captains who were part of this operation at the low end? No. But certainly it was in the mind of the Drina Corps Command at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's briefly go to P2199, another Drina Corps Command -- a document from the Drina Corps Command, forward command post. It's a regular combat report, and it's under the name of Major Milenko Jevdjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who Jevdjevic is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milenko Jevdjevic is the chief of Communications. I believe, if I recall correctly, he was the chief of Communications for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you explain why his name would be on a daily combat report from the Drina Corps, from the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in the context of the Main Staff sending officers down to subordinate command posts to observe the military actions, the corps did the same thing. It was not uncommon for the Drina Corps Command or any of the other corps to send corps staff officers down to subordinate brigade or lower formations in order to personally observe the operations that were being carried out and to ensure that they were being carried out in compliance with the orders from, in this case, the corps command. So the fact that Major Jevdjevic would be there as part of a forward command post and would write this report is not remarkable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just call your attention, in the first page of the document, to the Drina Corps -- to the Command of the Drina Corps, to the chief of staff personally. And the chief of staff at that time was who of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe at that time the chief of staff was -- June, it would probably still be Colonel Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says: "After a successful operation and the forceful expulsion of UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post, the enemy was observed building up large forces and moving them from Srebrenica sector towards the general sector of Zeleni Jadar. Their formation included two armoured personnel carriers and one tank." Did the Muslims ever have armoured personnel carriers or a tank that was actively being used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember a Drina Corps formation called the 5th Communications Battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember who the chief of that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I just got confused. Nedjo Blagojevic was the chief of communications, which meant Milenko Jevdjevic would have been the commander of the 5th Communications Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what does this first sentence indicate to you? Is it, in your view, related at all to General Zivanovic's instructions on how to approach an OP? And I mean after the successful operation and forceful expulsion of UNPROFOR from the Zeleni Jadar post.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I understand that particular question. If you could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does this sentence mean? What do you think it's referring to, aside from the obvious? Is it related to the previous order of General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's related to the order in so much as it's reporting about events in Zeleni Jadar and around Zeleni Jadar after they have captured it, and what, in this respect, given where it's relating to the enemy, they're talking about a potential build-up of what might be a counter-attack force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And going to the next page in English, it should be near the -- it's identified as paragraph 3 right near the bottom of the document in B/C/S. Probably have to go to the next page in the B/C/S. Yes. Number 3, it says in the English: "We have had no casualties. We have expended small amounts of ammunition and three Zoljas," which the interpreters say are hand-held rocket-launchers. Can you tell us what your understanding of a Zolja is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a manned portable rocket-launcher primarily used for anti-armour purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it anything like what we've heard of an RPG, rocket-propelled grenade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we look back to the Zivanovic document, P625, we see, referring to UNPROFOR: "If they do not comply with this order, fire a hand-held rocket-launcher" - "Zolja," actually, is what he said - "at the generator, and be ready to neutralise the APC," the armoured personnel carrier, "paying attention to not hurt physically UNPROFOR soldiers." So firing a Zolja at a generator or an APC, how significant is that to the members of the APC crew or the OP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're firing at a stand-alone generator, you're going to get hit, you're going to lose electricity. Depending on where the generator is, it's going to appear, potentially, that you're being fired on directly. When you're firing at an APC and there's a crew inside the armoured personnel carrier, they're certainly going to take it as they are being directly attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer that into evidence, 2199. Oh, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see a "P" in front now. Thank you. All right. If we could go now to 65 ter 4034. It should be 78. I've skipped one on the -- in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that this is a Main Staff Security and Intelligence Sector document from Chief Major General Zdravko Tolimir, is how the English translation has it. And can you tell us what this is? I don't need a whole lot of detail, but can you just tell us what purpose this serves, if any, in the work of the -- General Tolimir's sector? We see that it's sent to Forward Command Post 2 of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic personally. That's in the last page. Where is that, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, I believe this IKM is either physically in Banja Luka or somewhere in the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So just generally tell us what this is coming from General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- you know, just like the corps commands had to publish their daily operational reports, the Intelligence Sector -- Intelligence and Security Sector published a daily intel report which laid out, for a variety of customers, all of the relevant intelligence that had been collected, analysed, and was being again sent out for operational purposes by -- not only to the Main Staff, but to the civilian government, to the Ministry of the Interior, to the corps commanders, and to other customers which would include, in this particular instance, members of the Main Staff of the Serb Krajina Army, and, I believe at this juncture, even members of the Security Administration of the federal army in Belgrade. So this was their daily intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what I want to direct your attention to is page 4 in the English and probably about the last page or the second-to-the-last page -- second-to-the-last page, page 2, in the Serbian, and that middle paragraph in the English that begins: "In the area of Srebrenica," thank you, "there is increased distrust among the population in relation to the military and civilian leadership, and also accusations that they have caused the reprisal of the VRS by the infiltration and action of the sabotage and terrorist groups in Serbian territory. The 28th Division Command is circulating disinformation that the VRS carried out a sabotage attack on civilian features, wanting to cause condemnation by the international community. According to unverified information, they have blocked UNPROFOR units, accusing them that they are not protecting the so-called demilitarised zone." Now, this is dated June 25th, 1995. Are you aware, Mr. Butler, of any sabotage action by the 10th Sabotage Detachment into the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's quickly go to P961. And I see we're running out of time, but this is a UN document dated 24 June 1995, the day before the last one, and we see this, that it talks about a group of unknown strength came in through a mine and fired upon an area and killed a woman. Does this UN report have anything to do, to your knowledge, with this action by the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This particular document is describing the attack that took place by the 10th Sabotage Detachment, although, obviously, they're not aware of who the actual perpetrator was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if the 10th Sabotage Detachment, on the day before Tolimir's intelligence report, had gone into the enclave and made this attack, would this be a correct statement of General Tolimir, that the 28th Division Command is circulating disinformation about the VRS carrying out a sabotage attack on civilian features?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It raises one of two possibilities. The first possibility is that it is a form of disinformation, and given the fact that there are customers for this report outside the Republika Srpska, to influence their opinions in that regard. The second is that the person who drafted the report might not have been -- read into the fact that the 10th Sabotage had conducted this act and, in fact, it had occurred as such. One kind of discounts the second course of action only because somewhere along the line during the review process of this document, it should have reached a level where somebody who was aware of it, as obviously Colonel Salapura would and General Tolimir would be aware of it, would notice that, you know, that was incorrect and direct it to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "this is disinformation," what do you mean is disinformation or could be disinformation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Disinformation," in a military sense, is the production of incorrect or false or misleading materials or statements that are designed to cause an adversary to look in a different direction, to focus resources in a different area, or even, in a more political sense, to hold an opinion that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So would General Tolimir be sending disinformation out to possibly these -- his own people or other entities, as the address list shows?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this into evidence, 65 ter 4034.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4034 shall be assigned Exhibit P2512. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the UN document is already in evidence. And we're five minutes past, but I'm told there's nobody after us, so I don't think we've interfered with anyone. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will continue our hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 13th day of July, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
